Today Instance is launching and showcasing their success detector for robot policies — the first piece of what will eventually be fully automated robot evaluation. You can try it now at demo.instancelabs.ai. Describe a task, upload a video (or record one on your phone), and it judges whether the robot actually did the thing.

Instance is @clairemao78 and @lucyjcai. They're MIT-trained computer scientists who've been friends since middle school. Lucy did humanoid robotics research in MIT's Learning and Intelligent Systems lab, wrote collision-avoidance software at SpaceX that handled the entire Starlink fleet, and built Amazon's first LLM-based unit test generation at AWS. Claire wrote planetary atmosphere simulation software at NASA JPL and did propulsion research at the MIT Media Lab. I met them at the end of last year, and it’s been a pleasure working with them as they iterated through their ideas and landed on this product.

The idea came from Lucy's research on robots. To achieve her results, she spent a year babysitting a robot: start a rollout, watch a humanoid open drawers for 30 minutes, mark success or fail in a spreadsheet, get up, reset the room, do it again. That's one robot in one lab. Industry teams run fleets of robots across dozens of policies, and today the answer is literally people sitting in chairs watching them. Every robotics team they've talked to has some version of this problem, and it gets worse as robot foundation models scale.

So they built the judge. Give it a task description and rollout footage, and it returns a success verdict with subtask-level captions. They benchmarked it on 10,000+ held-out, human-labeled episodes across 7 robot platforms, and it beats a frontier VLM on accuracy at a fraction of the latency. They also bought their own robot arm and are training policies on it.

Every big leap in AI has been unlocked by cheap, scalable feedback — and robotics doesn't have that yet. Right now, knowing whether a robot actually did its job still takes a human watching it. That's the bottleneck, and it only gets more painful as the field scales. Whoever removes it ends up sitting somewhere very fundamental in the stack — not a tool robotics teams use, but a layer they build on. The end state Instance is working toward is an evaluation loop with no humans in it at all: your robot rolls out, Instance judges it, a second robot resets the scene, next rollout starts. However robotics unfolds from here, that loop gets more valuable, not less. I think it's these two.

If you're training robot policies, running evals, or deploying robots in the real world, email founders@instancelabs.ai. They'll come to your office with sweet treats and show you.

This week Prized is launching publicly. Watch the launch video — it's a good one — or just go try the product.

Prized lets anyone at a company build and ship internal tools with AI. Not just engineers. The ops person, the support lead, the finance analyst — the people who actually understand the workflow. They describe the tool they need, and Prized builds it on top of the right company data, deploys it behind the company's sign-in, and keeps every data access scoped and audited.

I'm @itsmarinos and @hudson_gri's group partner at YC, and I've had the pleasure of working with them in this batch. They're two of the strongest product people in my group. This isn't a hunch — everything they ship, from the landing page to the demo to the launch video (which they edited themselves in a day), has unusual taste for a two-person team a few weeks in.

They earned this problem the hard way. Hudson was the first engineer at Gander (YC F24), joining before there was a codebase and staying through its acquisition by Archer Aviation. He then built internal AI tooling at Suno. Marinos was on the same Gander team while studying CS and Mechanical Engineering at Stanford, where he also TA'd the two largest CS courses on campus. At Gander they lived the internal-tools problem from the engineering side: the people who most needed dashboards, lookups, and approval flows were exactly the people who couldn't build them.

Those people aren't waiting on engineering anymore. They're pulling company data into Claude Code and Cursor and shipping tools in an afternoon — with no permissions, no audit trail, and no one watching where the data goes. The tool is "just internal," so security is assumed. It isn't.

Prized's answer is to make the safe path the easy path. Security is enforced in the infrastructure, not left to whoever built the tool. Every tool gets least-privilege access to only the data it was granted. Credentials live in a broker and never touch the tool's code. Outbound calls go through a controlled proxy. IT sees every tool in the org — who built it, what it touches, who uses it — and risky changes need explicit approval before they ship.

I think the interesting long-term piece is what happens after the first tool. One employee publishes a tool, a teammate forks it and points it at their own data, and over time the company builds a library of governed software it actually owns. Companies have always been full of people who know exactly what software they need. For the first time, they can build it themselves without creating a security problem.

If you work in ops, support, finance, or RevOps and keep waiting on engineering for small tools — or you're on a security team worried about where those tools are already being built — reach out: founders@prized.dev.

Geoffrey Moore says startups die in the chasm because pragmatist buyers demand a "whole product." These folks won't tolerate gaps. They need references. They need the complete solution. The chasm is lethal because because the buyers won't buy without perfection.

But Moore's model assumes there's an EXISTING solution the buyer is comparing you to. The whole framework assumes the buyer has a status quo they're comfortable with.

When the *bar is zero*, when the alternative is literally "we die" or "we do this entirely by hand with 2,000 people" (Block's compliance team) or "we just don't have this capability at all"?  

The chasm doesn't exist for those. 

Buyers start acting like visionaries instead of skeptics, because they have to buy. The alternative doesn't exist. They'll tolerate a 60% solution, missing features, no references, because 60% of something beats 100% of nothing.

The companies I get most excited about aren't disrupting incumbents. They're filling voids. 9 Mothers in the YC Spring 2026 batch is a counter-drone defense co for whom bar is zero, there is no viable close quarters defense otherwise! There's no chasm to cross for that. 

The practical implication for founders: if you're in a market where the bar is zero, stop worrying about whole product, stop worrying about crossing the chasm, stop worrying about pragmatist references. Ship the 60% solution. They're begging for it.

If you're NOT in a bar-is-zero market (if there's an incumbent, a status quo, a "good enough") then Moore applies in full and you need the whole playbook (beachhead, bowling alley, whole product, the works).

The question every founder should ask: is my customer's current alternative literally nothing? If yes, you're in a different game than the textbooks describe. Ship it in whatever form you have. You'll know. And it's a great place to be.
